title: Understanding Labor Pain
learningGoals: Explain why labor hurts, and how contractions come in waves
Understand how fear and tension can make pain feel worse
Know what can make labor pain easier or harder to cope with
Know the full range of comfort options, medical and non-medical
Tell the difference between coping and not coping, and what to do

review.notes: Drafted 2026-10-18 as lesson 3.1, the first lesson of Module 3 (Comfort, Movement, and Support Skills), in a new course folder. Builds on Labor Basics lesson 3 (stages of labor) and lesson 4.3 (medical pain relief); breathing, positions, touch and water, and support are covered in lessons 3.2 to 3.5. Sources were found by web search only; this session could not open the pages, so every source needs to be opened and confirmed. For the reviewer: the causes of labor pain (the uterus tightening, the cervix opening, the baby pressing down and stretching tissues) and that the pain stops between contractions follow the Lamaze article on labor pain; the fear-tension-pain cycle and the roles of oxytocin and endorphins are from Lamaze, not confirmed against an ACOG source; what makes pain easier or harder (support, movement, feeling safe; fear, being alone, lying flat, exhaustion, a baby facing up) draws on Lamaze and Committee Opinion 766; the signs of coping and not coping are a common childbirth-education framing not confirmed word for word in these sources. Reviewer decisions (Bryan Kurtz MD, FACOG, 2026-10-18): keep why labor hurts, 'this pain has a purpose', and 'often with no pain at all' between contractions; keep the fear-tension cycle with oxytocin and endorphins; keep what makes pain easier or harder, including a baby facing up; keep the coping and not-coping signs; keep the Module 3 title and home-screen line; no video for this lesson.

slides.heading: Understanding Labor Pain
onScreen: Module 3: Comfort, Movement, and Support Skills
slides.narration: Welcome to Module 3, Comfort, Movement, and Support Skills. Many people's biggest question about labor is how much it will hurt, and how they'll cope. In this first lesson, we'll look at why labor hurts, what makes it easier or harder, and the full range of ways to find comfort. The rest of this module is hands-on, with skills you can practice.

visual.description: A pregnant person sitting on a birth ball in a calm living room, eyes closed and breathing slowly, while their support partner sits behind them with hands resting gently on their shoulders. No readable writing.

slides.heading: Why labor hurts
onScreen: Your uterus tightens with each contraction
Your cervix stretches open
Your baby presses down and stretches the birth canal
This pain has a purpose: it's bringing your baby
slides.narration: Labor pain comes from real, hard work. With each contraction, the muscles of your uterus tighten. Your cervix stretches open. And as your baby moves down, they press on and stretch the tissues of the birth canal. Unlike pain from an injury, labor pain has a purpose. It's a sign your body is working to bring your baby.

visual.description: Three simple icons with short labels: a heartbeat line for the uterus tightening, an open circle for the cervix opening, and a baby for the baby moving down.

slides.heading: Pain comes in waves
onScreen: Each contraction builds, peaks, and fades
Then there's a break, often with no pain at all
Contractions get longer and stronger as labor goes on
Take them one at a time
slides.narration: Labor pain comes in waves. Each contraction builds, peaks, and then fades. Then there's a break, often with no pain at all, where you can rest and gather your strength. As labor goes on, contractions usually get longer, stronger, and closer together, and the breaks get shorter. Many people find it helps to take them one at a time, and to use each break to fully relax.

visual.description: Three stacked steps for one contraction: it builds, it peaks, then a break to rest.

slides.heading: Fear, tension, and pain
onScreen: Fear can make you tense up
Tension can make pain feel worse
Relaxing, knowing what to expect, and support help
Your body also makes its own pain relievers
slides.narration: How you feel can change how pain feels. When you're afraid, it's natural to tense up, and tension can make pain feel stronger, which can make you more afraid. Knowing what to expect, relaxing your body, and having support can help break that cycle. Your body helps, too. It makes oxytocin, which keeps contractions going, and endorphins, natural chemicals that ease pain.

visual.description: A laboring person standing and leaning on a counter with relaxed, dropped shoulders and a loose jaw, eyes closed, while their support partner gently rubs their lower back. Calm, softly lit room. No readable writing.

question.prompt: During a contraction, you notice your shoulders are up and your hands are clenched. What might help?
options: Tense up more to push through it
Drop your shoulders, loosen your hands, and breathe out slowly
Hold your breath until it's over
question.explanation: Tension can make pain feel worse. Dropping your shoulders, loosening your hands and jaw, and breathing out slowly can help.

slides.heading: What makes it easier, or harder
onScreen: Easier: support, feeling safe, moving, and rest between contractions
Harder: fear, being alone, lying flat, and exhaustion
Your baby's position matters too
Everyone's labor feels different
slides.narration: Many things affect how labor feels. It's often easier when you have continuous support, feel safe, can move and change positions, and rest between contractions. It's often harder when you're frightened, alone, lying flat on your back, or exhausted. Your baby's position matters too. If your baby is facing up, you may feel more pain in your back. And everyone's labor feels different, so there's no right way to feel.

visual.description: A laboring person walking slowly down a quiet hospital hallway, holding their support partner's arm and smiling, while a nurse walks nearby. No readable writing or signs.

slides.heading: The full range of comfort options
onScreen: Without medicine: breathing, movement, touch, water, and support
With medicine: an epidural, IV pain medicine, or nitrous oxide
Many people use a mix
You can change your mind as labor goes
slides.narration: There's a full range of ways to find comfort. Without medicine, there's breathing, movement and positions, touch and massage, warm water, and continuous support. You'll practice these in the rest of this module. With medicine, there's an epidural, IV pain medicine, or nitrous oxide, which you learned about in Module 4. Many people use a mix, starting with comfort skills and adding medicine later, or not. You can change your mind as labor goes.

visual.description: Six simple icons with short labels: wind for breathing, a standing person for movement, a heart with a handshake for touch and support, a shower head for water, a syringe for an epidural, and a pill for IV medicine.

slides.heading: Coping, not pain-free
onScreen: The goal is coping, not zero pain
Coping: finding a rhythm, and relaxing between contractions
Not coping: panic, tension, or feeling unable to go on
If you're not coping, change something
slides.narration: For many people, the goal isn't zero pain. It's coping. You're coping when you find a rhythm, like a breath, a sound, or a movement, and can relax between contractions. You may not be coping if you feel panicked, stay tense between contractions, or feel you can't go on. That's a signal to change something: a new position, more support, a shower, or medical pain relief. All of these are good choices.

visual.description: A laboring person swaying slowly with their arms around their support partner's neck in a slow dance, both calm and in rhythm, in a softly lit hospital room. No readable writing.

slides.heading: Your thoughts about labor pain
onScreen: What worries you most about labor pain
What helps you cope with pain or stress now
One comfort option you'd like to try
slides.narration: Let's take a moment. What worries you most about labor pain? What already helps you cope with pain or stress, like music, a warm shower, or a hand to hold? And what's one comfort option you'd like to try in labor? Save your answers to your Birth Readiness Brief, and share them with your support person.
slides.prompt: Write what worries you about labor pain, what helps you cope with pain or stress now, and one comfort option you'd like to try.

slides.heading: What we covered
onScreen: Labor pain comes from your body's work, and comes in waves
Fear and tension can make pain worse; relaxing and support help
Comfort options range from breathing and movement to an epidural
Aim to cope, and change something if you're not
slides.narration: Let's recap. Labor pain comes from the work of contractions, your cervix opening, and your baby moving down, and it comes in waves with breaks in between. Fear and tension can make pain worse, while relaxing and support help. Comfort options range from breathing and movement to an epidural. And the goal is coping, so if you're not, change something. Next up, a few review questions.

reviewQuiz.prompt: What makes labor pain different from pain from an injury?
options: It has a purpose, and comes in waves with breaks between
It only happens in the back
reviewQuiz.explanation: Labor pain comes from your body's work to bring your baby, and it comes in waves, often with no pain between contractions.

reviewQuiz.prompt: How can fear affect labor pain?
options: Fear can make you tense, and tension can make pain feel worse
reviewQuiz.explanation: Fear can lead to tension, which can make pain feel stronger. Knowing what to expect, relaxing, and support can help.

reviewQuiz.prompt: You feel panicked and can't relax between contractions. What's a good step?
options: Keep going exactly as you are
Change something: a new position, more support, a shower, or medical pain relief
Lie flat and hold your breath
reviewQuiz.explanation: Panic and constant tension are signs you may not be coping. Changing something, including choosing medical pain relief, is a good choice.
